description: Viking sagas, mystery plays, the Elizabethan playhouse, Victorian music halls and glee clubs.
content_html:
Viking Sagas and Anglo-Saxon Performance

Long before permanent theatres existed in Britain, sagas and epic poems provided entertainment in the great halls of the early medieval period. Travelling performers — known as scops in Anglo-Saxon culture — recited long narrative poems from memory, accompanied by a harp. The Old English epic poem Beowulf, composed some time between the seventh and tenth centuries, is the most famous surviving example. It tells the story of a Geatish hero who defeats the monster Grendel, and its performance context was the communal hall.

Viking culture brought its own tradition of saga performance to Britain. Norse sagas combined heroic narrative, mythological content and genealogical history. Performance was communal, participatory and central to identity. There were no buildings dedicated to performance: the hall, the church, and later the market square served as informal venues.

Medieval Mystery Plays

Mystery plays were the dominant form of popular drama in medieval England. They dramatised stories from the Bible, from Creation to the Last Judgement, in a cycle of short plays performed by the town guilds on wagons in a sequence of stops around the town centre. The York Mystery Plays and the Chester Mystery Plays are the best-documented surviving cycles. Performances took place on the feast of Corpus Christi, providing religious instruction through entertainment.

The guilds took great pride in their performances: the shipwrights typically played the story of Noah’s Ark; the bakers, the Last Supper. Costumes and props became elaborate, and performances could draw large crowds. Mummers also provided dramatic entertainment, particularly at Christmas: troupes of masked performers enacted folk dramas, often involving a symbolic death-and-resurrection narrative.

Key Fact

Medieval mystery plays were performed on wagons by town guilds on the feast of Corpus Christi. The York and Chester cycles are the most important surviving examples. They combined religious instruction with popular entertainment, making Bible stories accessible to people who could not read.

The Elizabethan Playhouse

The opening of the first permanent public theatre in London — simply called The Theatre — in Shoreditch in 1576 marks a decisive moment in English cultural history. Within two decades, a thriving commercial theatre industry had emerged in the suburbs of London, outside the jurisdiction of the city authorities who disapproved of theatre as immoral and disruptive.

The most famous of the Elizabethan playhouses was the Globe Theatre, built in Southwark in 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain’s Men, the company that included William Shakespeare as both playwright and sharer. The Globe was a large, open-air, three-tiered circular structure accommodating perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 spectators. Admission was as little as a penny for standing room in the pit, making theatre genuinely accessible to ordinary Londoners — apprentices, craftsmen and servant girls attended alongside the wealthy in the galleries.

The plays performed in Elizabethan theatre ranged from Shakespeare’s tragedies and histories to the comedies of Ben Jonson and the tragedies of Christopher Marlowe. Performance depended on spoken language, elaborate costume and convention rather than scenery, because the open-air stage had no ability to change lighting. Cross-dressing was necessary because women were barred from the stage — all female roles were played by boy actors.

The Puritan-dominated Parliament closed all public theatres in 1642 as ungodly and disruptive. They remained closed for eighteen years. When Charles II was restored to the throne in 1660, he brought back a taste for European theatrical culture, including painted scenery, indoor candlelit theatres and, for the first time, professional women actors on the English stage. Restoration theatre was initially an elite affair, attracting the court and the fashionable classes, but it gradually spread to broader urban audiences.

Victorian Music Halls

The music hall was the defining entertainment venue of Victorian Britain. Growing out of pub concert rooms in the 1840s, dedicated music hall buildings were constructed across British towns and cities. By 1866, London alone had around 30 large music halls and over 200 smaller venues. The entertainment was fast-paced, populist and participatory: comic singers, acrobats, jugglers, magicians and sentimental balladeers performed in rotation before audiences who ate, drank and sang along.

Star performers became the celebrities of their age. Marie Lloyd, whose career reached its peak in the 1890s, was one of the most famous music hall entertainers in Britain, known for comic songs with risqué undertones that commented on working-class life. Albert Chevalier and Dan Leno were equally celebrated. Music halls provided the model for later variety theatre, the circus, and ultimately the format of television light entertainment.

Alongside music halls, glee clubs represented a more respectable strand of musical entertainment. They originated in the eighteenth century as male singing societies, performing harmonised part-songs. By the nineteenth century the tradition had broadened: choral societies proliferated across industrial towns, particularly in the north and Wales. The Huddersfield Choral Society, founded in 1836, is one of the most famous surviving examples. Choral singing gave working-class people a respected cultural activity that crossed religious and political lines.

Key Fact

Music halls were Victorian variety entertainment venues that grew from pub concert rooms in the 1840s. By the 1860s London had over 200 such venues. Stars like Marie Lloyd became nationally celebrated. Music halls were the dominant popular entertainment of the late Victorian period until the rise of cinema.
exam_tip_html: For a question on ‘popular entertainment’, span the full chronological range. The examiner expects you to move from Viking sagas and mystery plays to Elizabethan theatre to Victorian music halls as a continuous story of change. Remember to consider what stayed the same: popular entertainment was always communal, participatory and tied to the places where people gathered — first the hall and market square, then the playhouse, then the music hall. An 8-mark significance answer should address both contemporary and longer-term significance of the venue or performer you discuss.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval entertainment moved from oral saga performance in halls (Anglo-Saxon scops, Viking sagas) to the organised drama of mystery plays performed by guilds on feast days.
  • The Elizabethan playhouse (Globe Theatre, 1599) created a commercial, accessible theatre industry; admission cost as little as a penny, making it open to all social classes.
  • Victorian music halls (from the 1840s) became the dominant popular entertainment venue, producing national celebrities like Marie Lloyd and laying the foundations for modern light entertainment.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of mystery plays in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. performed on wagons by town guilds on the feast of Corpus Christi / dramatised Bible stories from Creation to the Last Judgement / the York and Chester cycles are the most famous surviving examples. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Elizabethan playhouse.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. open-air, circular, three-tiered structures accommodating thousands of spectators (feature + detail of the Globe in Southwark); penny admission in the pit made theatre accessible to all social classes including apprentices and craftsmen (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why theatre became popular with ordinary Londoners in the Elizabethan period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking penny admission, central Southwark location, range of content (tragedy, comedy, history) and performance quality to broad popular appeal; evidence-based. Secure: Clear explanation with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the closure of theatres by Parliament in 1642.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. eighteen years of suppression ended the tradition of public outdoor theatre; when theatres reopened in 1660, the Restoration format was different (indoor, women on stage, scenic). Specific evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant were music halls in the development of popular entertainment in Victorian Britain?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (dominant entertainment venue, national celebrities, 200+ London halls by 1860s) AND over time (model for variety theatre, television light entertainment format). Uses evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Popular entertainment in Britain became increasingly accessible to ordinary people between c.500 and 1900.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement tracing accessibility across all three eras. Agrees: mystery plays (communal/free), penny admission at Globe, mass music halls. Challenges: Elizabethan theatre still excluded women from the stage; music halls catered to urban workers, not rural poor. Weighs change vs continuity. Overall conclusion. Secure: Evidence from at least two eras, some weighing. Developing: Limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What were mystery plays, and when were they typically performed in medieval England?
options: Plays about Norse myths, performed at the winter solstice
Bible-based dramas performed by town guilds on the feast of Corpus Christi
Royal entertainments performed at court during Christmas
Greek tragedies revived by Renaissance scholars

knowledge_checks.q: How much did it cost to stand in the pit at the Globe Theatre in Elizabethan London?
Victorian _____ halls grew from pub concert rooms in the 1840s and became the dominant popular entertainment venue of the late Victorian period.
The Globe Theatre was built in Southwark in _____ by the Lord Chamberlain's Men.
Match each form of entertainment to its era or description:
right: Masked folk performers enacting seasonal dramas, often at Christmas
Open-air circular theatres built in London from the 1570s
Male social singing societies performing harmonised part-songs

flashcard_questions.q: What were sagas in Viking and Anglo-Saxon culture?
flashcard_questions.a: Oral narrative poems performed by professional storytellers, recounting heroic deeds and mythology.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Beowulf, and when was it composed?
flashcard_questions.a: An Old English epic poem about a hero defeating a monster, composed between the seventh and tenth centuries.
Bible-based dramas performed by town guilds on wagons on the feast of Corpus Christi.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two most famous surviving medieval mystery play cycles.
flashcard_questions.a: The York Mystery Plays and the Chester Mystery Plays.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Globe Theatre built, and who built it?
flashcard_questions.a: 1599, by the Lord Chamberlain's Men in Southwark.

flashcard_questions.q: Who played female roles in Elizabethan theatre, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Boy actors — women were barred from the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to English theatres in 1642, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Parliament closed them as ungodly; they remained shut for eighteen years.

flashcard_questions.q: When did women first appear professionally on the English stage?
flashcard_questions.a: After the Restoration of Charles II in 1660.
Victorian variety entertainment venues offering comic songs, acrobatics and juggling, growing from pub concert rooms in the 1840s.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one famous Victorian music hall performer.
flashcard_questions.a: Marie Lloyd (or Albert Chevalier / Dan Leno).
Social singing clubs for men performing harmonised part-songs, popular in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Huddersfield Choral Society, and when was it founded?
flashcard_questions.a: A famous Victorian choral society founded in 1836.

glossary_terms.definition: Oral narrative poems performed by professional storytellers in Viking and Anglo-Saxon culture, recounting heroic deeds, mythology and history.
Dramatic performances based on stories from the Bible, performed in medieval English towns on feast days such as Corpus Christi, typically organised by the town guilds.
Performers who acted out folk stories and seasonal customs in masks and disguises, often at Christmas and on feast days, as a form of community ritual.
Open-air, circular theatres built in Elizabethan London from the 1570s, accommodating audiences of all social classes.
Venues providing popular variety entertainment including comic songs, acrobatics, juggling and dance, that flourished in Victorian Britain from the 1840s.
Social singing clubs for men, popular in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, that met to perform part-songs and catches in informal settings.
